// HR Analytics — All Measures table
// Reconstructed from the measure names and visual bindings in HR_Analytics.pbix.
// The original DAX is inside the compressed model and could not be read, so
// these are the standard definitions for this dataset. Column names follow the
// public HR Analytics sample (Employee, PerformanceRating, *Level lookup tables).
// Adjust names if your columns differ.

// ---------- Headline KPIs (six cards on every page) ----------

Total_Employee =
DISTINCTCOUNT ( Employee[EmployeeID] )

Attrition =
CALCULATE ( [Total_Employee], Employee[Attrition] = "Yes" )

Attrition% =
DIVIDE ( [Attrition], [Total_Employee], 0 )

Retrenched% =
DIVIDE (
    CALCULATE ( [Total_Employee], Employee[Retrenched] = "Yes" ),
    [Total_Employee],
    0
)

Due for Promotion % =
DIVIDE (
    CALCULATE ( [Total_Employee], Employee[YearsSinceLastPromotion] >= 4 ),
    [Total_Employee],
    0
)

Avg_Salary =
AVERAGE ( Employee[Salary] )

Avg_Age =
AVERAGE ( Employee[Age] )

// ---------- Satisfaction and rating averages (Ratings page) ----------

Avg_Env_Sat =
AVERAGE ( PerformanceRating[EnvironmentSatisfaction] )

Avg_Job_Sat =
AVERAGE ( PerformanceRating[JobSatisfaction] )

Avg_Relation_Sat =
AVERAGE ( PerformanceRating[RelationshipSatisfaction] )

Avg_Work_Bal =
AVERAGE ( PerformanceRating[WorkLifeBalance] )

Avg_Manager_Rat =
AVERAGE ( PerformanceRating[ManagerRating] )

Avg_Self_Rat =
AVERAGE ( PerformanceRating[SelfRating] )

// ---------- Calculated columns used by the slicers and charts ----------

// Employee[Age Group]
Age Group =
SWITCH (
    TRUE (),
    Employee[Age] < 20, "<20",
    Employee[Age] < 30, "20-29",
    Employee[Age] < 40, "30-39",
    Employee[Age] < 50, "40-49",
    "50+"
)

// Employee[Dist_from_Home]
Dist_from_Home =
SWITCH (
    TRUE (),
    Employee[DistanceFromHome (KM)] <= 10, "0-10 km",
    Employee[DistanceFromHome (KM)] <= 20, "11-20 km",
    Employee[DistanceFromHome (KM)] <= 30, "21-30 km",
    "30+ km"
)

// ---------- Calendar table (data generation in Power Query or DAX) ----------

Calendar =
ADDCOLUMNS (
    CALENDAR ( MIN ( Employee[HireDate] ), MAX ( PerformanceRating[ReviewDate] ) ),
    "Year", YEAR ( [Date] ),
    "Month", FORMAT ( [Date], "MMM" ),
    "MonthNo", MONTH ( [Date] )
)

blocks.text: Power BI turns disconnected operational data into a shared view of what happened, why it happened, and what should happen next.

items.title: Descriptive
items.text: What happened?

items.title: Diagnostic
items.text: Why did it happen?

items.title: Predictive
items.text: What may happen next?

blocks.text: Raw data is a record of events. Business intelligence adds structure, context, and a visual language so teams can act. A useful report makes the important signal obvious without hiding the underlying detail, and it uses definitions everyone in the business agrees on.

head: Layer
Question
Typical Power BI output
rows: KPI cards, trend lines, monthly matrix
Forecast line, what-if parameter, ML score column
Scenario page, target vs actual, action-oriented tooltips

blocks.text: Where an analyst actually spends time

In real projects roughly 60% of effort goes into understanding the question and cleaning data, 25% into the model and calculations, and only 15% into visual design. Reports fail far more often because of unclear definitions than because of chart colours.

blocks.title: Working principle
blocks.text: Begin with a decision, not a chart. Ask what the reader needs to know or do after seeing the report, then work backwards to the data required.

items: 1. Write down three decisions your report should support, in one sentence each.
2. For each decision, name the single metric that would change the decision.
3. List the source systems where that metric lives today.
BI is a definition problem before it is a tooling problem.
Each report page should map to one question a stakeholder actually asks.
Descriptive reporting must be trustworthy before predictive work is worth attempting.

blocks.text: Power BI is Microsoft’s business analytics platform for connecting, preparing, modeling, visualizing, and sharing data.

items: Connect
Transform
Model
Visualize
Share
**Power BI Desktop** — free Windows authoring tool where models and reports are built.
**Power BI Service** — the cloud workspace that publishes, shares, refreshes, and governs content.
**Power BI Mobile** — phone and tablet consumption, including optimized phone layouts.
**Power BI Report Server** — on-premises hosting for organizations that cannot publish to the cloud.
**On-premises data gateway** — the secure bridge between local sources and the cloud service.

head: Engine
Language
Job
rows: Connect and reshape data before it lands in the model
Compress, store, and calculate over the model

head: License
What it allows
When to choose it
rows: Build in Desktop, publish to My Workspace only
Share workspaces and apps with other Pro users
Most teams and job-ready portfolio work
Larger models, more refreshes, advanced features

items: Desktop authors, Service distributes; keep the two roles clear in your head.
M shapes data, DAX calculates over the finished model.
Sharing beyond My Workspace requires at least Pro on both sides.

blocks.text: One model can combine spreadsheets, databases, cloud warehouses, web APIs, and business applications.

items: Excel & CSV files
SQL Server, Postgres, MySQL
Azure Synapse, Snowflake, BigQuery
SharePoint, Dataverse, SaaS APIs

head: Mode
How it works
Trade-off
rows: Data is compressed into the model file
Queries are sent to the source per visual
Near real-time, slower and limited DAX
Connects to an existing semantic model
One shared definition, no local modeling
Mix import tables with DirectQuery tables
Flexible, but requires careful storage design

items: Clarify the questions and agree metric definitions in writing.
Connect to the smallest useful set of source data.
Clean and shape it in Power Query with named steps.
Build a star schema, a date table, and reusable DAX measures.
Design report pages around questions, not around available fields.
Publish, secure with row-level security, schedule refresh, and iterate.

blocks.title: Naming discipline
blocks.text: Rename queries, columns, and measures in business language on day one. Renaming after ten visuals reference a field is far more painful than doing it up front.

items: Choose the storage mode from the freshness requirement, not from habit.
Reduce columns and rows at the source before importing.
Every project follows the same five stages: connect, transform, model, visualize, share.

blocks.text: Power BI Desktop is a free Windows application. The Microsoft Store version updates automatically and is the easiest option for most learners.

items.title: Microsoft Store
items.text: Automatic monthly updates and a straightforward installation path.

items.title: Direct download
items.text: Choose the 64-bit installer unless your organization requires another version.

items: **macOS** — run Windows in Parallels, UTM, or a cloud Windows 365 / Azure VM.
**Any OS** — author simple reports directly in the Power BI Service in a browser.
Keep the .pbix file on a synced folder so you can move between machines safely.
Sign in only if you need to publish to a workspace.
Open **File → Options and settings → Options** and review Data Load defaults.
Turn off *Auto date/time* — you will build a proper date table instead.
Confirm regional settings so dates and decimals parse correctly.
Review preview features, but avoid enabling them for production work.
Desktop is Windows-only; everything else is a workaround.
Disable auto date/time immediately to avoid hidden date tables.
Locale settings cause more parsing bugs than any other setting.

blocks.text: The Desktop workspace has three core views. Switching between them separates presentation, data inspection, and model design.

items.label: View
items.title: Report
items.text: Build pages and visuals

items.label: View
items.title: Table
items.text: Inspect rows, columns, and measures

items.label: View
items.title: Model
items.text: Create and inspect relationships

items.title: Data pane
items.text: Every table, column, hierarchy, and measure in the model.

items.title: Visualizations pane
items.text: Chart types plus the fields and format sub-panes.

items.title: Filters pane
items.text: Visual, page, and report level filters, in that order of scope.

items.title: Selection & bookmarks
items.text: Layer order, visibility, and saved report states.

head: Shortcut
Action
rows: Copy a visual with all its formatting
Follow a report link or multi-select in slicers

blocks.title: Shortcut
blocks.text: Spend time in Model view before polishing charts. A clear model makes every later calculation and visual easier to trust.

items: Report, Table, and Model views map to the three stages of authoring.
Filter scope runs visual → page → report; know which one you edited.
Copying a finished visual is the fastest way to keep formatting consistent.

blocks.text: Power Query is the data preparation engine inside Power BI. Every transformation is recorded as a repeatable step rather than a one-time manual edit.

items: Set correct data types
Remove errors and duplicates
Split or merge columns
Pivot and unpivot values
Merge and append queries
Create conditional columns
Group and summarize rows
Extract text, date, and number parts

head: Operation
What it does
Use case
rows: Joins columns from another query on a key
Add department name to the employee table
Stacks rows from queries with the same shape
Combine 12 monthly files into one table

blocks.text: Unpivot: the single most useful trick

Source spreadsheets often have one column per month. Models need one row per month. Select the identifier columns, right-click, and choose **Unpivot other columns** to turn a wide report into a tall table that a star schema can consume.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Shape data as early as practical. Use Power Query for structural cleaning and DAX for analytical calculations that respond to report filters.

items: 1. Import a messy Excel export with merged headers and blank rows.
2. Promote headers, remove blanks, set types, and unpivot the month columns.
3. Rename every column in business language and Close & Apply.
Transformations are steps, so cleaning is repeatable on every refresh.
Merge adds columns; append adds rows.
Unpivot converts spreadsheet layouts into model-friendly tables.

blocks.text: Open the editor from **Home → Transform data**. The query list, data preview, formula bar, and Applied Steps work together.

items: Rename the query and confirm the source path or connection.
Promote headers and remove empty rows.
Set explicit data types with locale where needed.
Remove columns the model will not use.
Standardize labels, trim whitespace, handle errors.
Review every Applied Step, then Close & Apply.

blocks.code:
// Power Query M example
let
  Source = Excel.Workbook(File.Contents("C:\\data\\hr.xlsx"), null, true),
  Employee = Source{[Item="Employee",Kind="Sheet"]}[Data],
  Headers = Table.PromoteHeaders(Employee, [PromoteAllScalars=true]),
  Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(
    Headers,
    {{"EmployeeID", Int64.Type}, {"HireDate", type date}, {"Salary", Currency.Type}}
  ),
  Cleaned = Table.SelectRows(Typed, each [EmployeeID] <> null)
in
  Cleaned

blocks.text: When a source is a database, Power Query tries to translate your steps into a single SQL statement — this is *query folding*, and it keeps refresh fast. Right-click a step and check **View Native Query**. Steps that break folding (custom M functions, added index columns) should sit as late in the chain as possible.

items: Create a **parameter** for the file or folder path so the report moves between machines.
Use a **staging query** with *Enable load* turned off, then reference it for each final table.
Group queries into folders: Sources, Staging, Model.
Applied Steps are your audit trail — name them meaningfully.
Keep folding alive as long as possible for database sources.
Parameters and staging queries make a project maintainable.

blocks.text: A refresh that silently drops rows is worse than one that fails loudly. Build checks into the query layer.

In the View ribbon enable **Column quality**, **Column distribution**, and **Column profile**, and switch profiling to the entire dataset instead of the first 1,000 rows. You are looking for unexpected blanks, outlier values, and columns where distinct count should equal row count.

head: Symptom
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Change type with locale, or replace errors
Group by key, or filter to current records
Replace values before setting the date type
Source filter or upstream schema change

items: 1. Add a query that returns the row count of each source table.
2. Load it into the model and place it on a hidden audit page.
3. Compare counts before and after your cleaning steps.
Profile the whole dataset, not the preview sample.
Handle errors explicitly instead of letting rows disappear.
An audit page turns silent data loss into a visible number.

blocks.text: A data model describes how tables relate. Good models reduce ambiguity, make calculations predictable, and keep reports fast.

items.title: Describe the business
items.text: Employee, department, date, geography — entities used to filter or group results.

items.title: Record events
items.text: Transactions, reviews, attendance, sales — measurable activity at a consistent grain.

blocks.text: Dimension tables surround a central fact table, each joined on a single key. This is easier to explain, produces simpler DAX, and usually performs better than one giant flat table or an over-normalized snowflake.

head: Design
Description
Verdict
rows: Facts in the middle, dimensions one hop away
Dimensions split into further lookup tables
Fine for a single quick view, bad at scale

blocks.text: Write the grain of every fact table as a sentence: “one row per employee per performance review.” If you cannot say it in one sentence, the table mixes grains and your measures will double count.

items: Facts measure, dimensions describe.
State the grain of each fact table in writing before modeling.
Star schema is the default; deviate only with a reason.

blocks.text: Relationships carry filters between tables. Cardinality and direction determine how visuals aggregate data.

items: A primary key uniquely identifies a dimension row.
A foreign key connects fact rows to that dimension.
Filters flow from the one side to the many side by default.
Use single-direction filtering unless the business case clearly needs both.
Only one relationship between two tables can be active at a time.

head: Type
Meaning
Notes
rows: Two tables share the same key
Prefer a bridge table for clarity

blocks.text: A fact table may have HireDate and ExitDate. Keep one active relationship to the date table and activate the other inside a measure with **USERELATIONSHIP**.

blocks.title: Ambiguity warning
blocks.text: If two paths connect the same tables, Power BI cannot decide which to use and will block the relationship. Redesign rather than forcing bi-directional filters.

items: Cardinality plus direction defines how filters travel.
Bi-directional filtering is a last resort, not a default.
USERELATIONSHIP handles multiple date roles cleanly.

blocks.text: Almost every time-intelligence bug traces back to a missing or badly marked date table.

items: One row per day, no gaps, covering every date in every fact table.
Whole years — 1 January to 31 December — so year-over-year works.
Marked with **Table tools → Mark as date table**.
Sort columns set so month names order correctly.

blocks.code:
Date =
VAR MinDate = MIN ( Employee[HireDate] )
VAR MaxDate = MAX ( Employee[HireDate] )
RETURN
ADDCOLUMNS (
  CALENDAR ( DATE ( YEAR ( MinDate ), 1, 1 ), DATE ( YEAR ( MaxDate ), 12, 31 ) ),
  "Year", YEAR ( [Date] ),
  "Quarter", "Q" & QUARTER ( [Date] ),
  "MonthNo", MONTH ( [Date] ),
  "Month", FORMAT ( [Date], "MMM" ),
  "YearMonth", FORMAT ( [Date], "YYYY-MM" ),
  "Weekday", FORMAT ( [Date], "ddd" ),
  "IsWorkday", IF ( WEEKDAY ( [Date], 2 ) <= 5, TRUE (), FALSE () )
)

blocks.text: Select the *Month* column, choose **Sort by column → MonthNo**. Without this, charts show April before January.

items: Continuous full-year date table, marked as a date table — non-negotiable.
Add MonthNo and set sort-by-column for readable axes.
Turn off auto date/time so hidden tables do not compete.

blocks.text: A tidy model is the difference between a report someone inherits happily and one they rebuild from scratch.

items.title: Hide technical fields
items.text: Hide keys and helper columns from report view so the field list only shows business terms.

items.title: Measure table
items.text: Create a blank table named _Measures and store every measure there.

items.title: Display folders
items.text: Group measures into folders such as Headcount, Attrition, Salary.

items.title: Formatting in the model
items.text: Set currency, percentage, and decimal places once on the measure.

blocks.text: Add a description to every measure explaining the definition and any exclusions. It appears as a tooltip in the field list and in the Service, and it prevents the “which attrition number is right?” conversation.

items: Hide everything a report author should not touch.
One measures table with display folders scales to hundreds of measures.
Measure descriptions are the cheapest documentation you will ever write.

blocks.text: DAX is the calculation language of the model. Learn three concepts — measures, calculated columns, and filter context — and most of the language follows.

blocks.code:
Total_Employee = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Employee[EmployeeID] )

Average Salary = AVERAGE ( Employee[MonthlyIncome] )

Attrition = CALCULATE ( [Total_Employee], Employee[Attrition] = "Yes" )

Attrition % = DIVIDE ( [Attrition], [Total_Employee], 0 )

Attrition % =
VAR Leavers = CALCULATE ( [Total_Employee], Employee[Attrition] = "Yes" )
VAR Headcount = [Total_Employee]
RETURN
DIVIDE ( Leavers, Headcount, 0 )

blocks.title: Style rules
blocks.text: Use DIVIDE instead of /. Use variables instead of repeating expressions. Reference measures by \[Name\] and columns by Table\[Name\] — always.

items: Measures respond to filters; calculated columns are fixed at refresh.
DIVIDE prevents divide-by-zero errors.
Variables improve both readability and performance.

blocks.text: CALCULATE is the only function that can change filter context. Understanding it is the real turning point in learning DAX.

items.title: Filter context
items.text: The set of filters applied by slicers, rows, columns, and CALCULATE when a measure evaluates.

items.title: Row context
items.text: The current row, present in calculated columns and inside iterators like SUMX.

blocks.text: SUMX, AVERAGEX, MAXX, and RANKX walk a table row by row, evaluating an expression in row context and then aggregating. Use them when the calculation must happen per row before aggregation.

blocks.code:
Total Comp = SUMX ( Employee, Employee[MonthlyIncome] * 12 )

Dept Rank =
RANKX ( ALL ( Department[Department] ), [Attrition %],, DESC )

items: Wrapping a column in a measure without an aggregation.
Using ALL when REMOVEFILTERS or ALLSELECTED is what you meant.
Building calculated columns that should have been measures.
Nesting CALCULATE three levels deep instead of using variables.
1. Build Attrition % and check that it stays correct when you slice by department.
2. Add % of Workforce and confirm the total sums to 100%.
3. Rank departments by attrition and show the top three in a card.
CALCULATE modifies filter context; everything else reacts to it.
REMOVEFILTERS and ALLEXCEPT control what a percentage compares against.
Iterators add row context when per-row math is required.

blocks.text: With a marked date table, time comparisons become one-line measures.

blocks.code:
Headcount YTD =
TOTALYTD ( [Total_Employee], 'Date'[Date] )

Headcount LY =
CALCULATE ( [Total_Employee], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )

YoY % =
DIVIDE ( [Total_Employee] - [Headcount LY], [Headcount LY] )

Rolling 3 Months =
CALCULATE (
  [Total_Employee],
  DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], MAX ( 'Date'[Date] ), -3, MONTH )
)

head: Need
Function
rows: Custom columns plus CALCULATE, not built-ins

blocks.title: Why it broke
blocks.text: If a time-intelligence measure returns blank, check three things in order: is the date table marked, does it cover full years, and are you filtering by the date table rather than the fact table's date column?

items: Time intelligence requires a marked, contiguous date table.
Always slice by the date dimension, never the fact date column.
Fiscal calendars usually need custom columns instead of built-in functions.

blocks.text: Match the chart to the comparison. Most confusing reports use the wrong encoding, not the wrong colours.

items: Sort bars by value unless the category has a natural order.
Start numeric axes at zero for bar charts.
Use one accent colour for the metric that matters; grey everything else.
Write titles as findings — “Attrition highest in Sales (24%)” beats “Attrition by department”.
Label directly on the chart instead of forcing legend lookups.
Pick the visual from the question, not from the visuals pane.
Colour is for meaning, not decoration.
Titles should state the conclusion.

blocks.text: A consistent page reads faster. Build a grid once, then reuse it on every page.

items.title: Header strip
items.text: Report name, page name, and the global slicers.

items.title: KPI row
items.text: Four to six cards with the headline numbers.

items.title: Main analysis
items.text: Two to three charts answering the page's question.

items.title: Detail
items.text: Table or matrix, or a drill-through target page.

items: **Theme JSON** — set fonts, colours, and default visual formatting once.
**Format painter** — copy formatting between visuals.
**Align and distribute** — snap visuals to a grid; turn on gridlines and snap-to-grid.
**Page size** — 16:9 for screens, or a custom canvas for dense operational views.
Contrast of at least 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for chart elements.
Do not rely on colour alone — add labels, shapes, or icons.
Set tab order in the Selection pane so keyboard users move logically.
Add alt text to every visual describing what it shows.
A reusable grid and theme make every page feel deliberate.
Alt text and tab order are part of finishing a report, not extras.
Consistency beats novelty for reports people use weekly.

blocks.text: Interactivity replaces twenty near-identical pages with one page that answers many questions.

items: Use dropdowns for long lists, buttons for two or three options, a relative-date slicer for time.
**Sync slicers** across pages from the View menu so filters persist.
Use **Edit interactions** to stop a visual from being cross-filtered.

blocks.text: Bookmarks capture filters, visibility, and selection. Combine with the Selection pane to build a filter pane that slides in, or to toggle between a chart and its underlying table using two buttons and two bookmarks.

items: Create a detail page and add the field you drill on to the Drill through well.
Right-click any visual on the summary page and choose the detail page.
Keep the automatic back button and show the filter context in the page title.

blocks.text: Create a small page, set its size to *Tooltip*, mark it as a tooltip page, then assign it in the tooltip section of any visual. Hovering shows a mini report instead of a raw number.

items: 1. Add synced department and year slicers across all pages.
2. Build a drill-through page showing individual employees.
3. Add a tooltip page with a small trend line for the hovered department.
Sync slicers so users do not re-filter on every page.
Bookmarks plus the Selection pane create app-like navigation.
Drill-through and tooltip pages keep detail off the summary page.

blocks.text: The capstone turns employee and performance data into a three-page HR analytics report.

items.title: Overview
items.text: Workforce, attrition, salary

items.title: Demography
items.text: Age, distance, department

items.title: Ratings
items.text: Satisfaction and performance

head: Table
Grain
Key fields
rows: EmployeeID, Department, JobRole, Attrition, MonthlyIncome, HireDate
One row per employee per review

blocks.text: Start with a stable KPI row: total employees, attrition, attrition rate, retrenchment rate, promotion due, and average salary. Keep definitions identical across every page — a metric that means two things on two pages destroys trust.

head: Metric
Definition
rows: Employees with years since last promotion ≥ 3

items: Agree metric definitions before building a single visual.
Three pages, three questions — no page without a purpose.
Write the grain of each table down; it prevents double counting.

blocks.text: Measures calculate in the current filter context. Create reusable measures instead of embedding business logic separately in each visual.

blocks.code:
Total_Employee = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Employee[EmployeeID] )

Attrition = CALCULATE ( [Total_Employee], Employee[Attrition] = "Yes" )

Attrition% = DIVIDE ( [Attrition], [Total_Employee], 0 )

Active_Employee = [Total_Employee] - [Attrition]

Promotion_Due =
CALCULATE ( [Total_Employee], Employee[YearsSinceLastPromotion] >= 3 )

Average_Salary = AVERAGE ( Employee[MonthlyIncome] )

Avg_Tenure = AVERAGE ( Employee[YearsAtCompany] )

Attrition% LY =
CALCULATE ( [Attrition%], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )

Attrition% Delta = [Attrition%] - [Attrition% LY]

Highest_Attrition_Dept =
VAR Ranked =
  TOPN ( 1, ALL ( Department[Department] ), [Attrition%], DESC )
RETURN
  MAXX ( Ranked, Department[Department] )

items: Use **DIVIDE** instead of the slash operator when the denominator may be zero.
Create explicit measures for every important business definition.
Format rates as percentages and money as currency in the model, not in each visual.
Keep all measures in a dedicated *\_Measures* table with display folders.
Add a description to each measure so the tooltip explains the definition.

blocks.title: Sanity checks
blocks.text: Drop every measure into a table visual with no filters and confirm the totals against a spreadsheet count. Then slice by department and confirm the parts sum to the whole.

items: One measure per business definition, reused everywhere.
Format and document measures in the model.
Validate totals unfiltered, then sliced, before designing pages.

blocks.text: Every page should answer a distinct question while sharing filters, KPI definitions, spacing, and visual hierarchy.
Lead with the KPI row, then attrition and promotion patterns by department, job role, and tenure band. Add a line chart of attrition rate by month with last-year comparison.

items: Cards: total employees, attrition, attrition %, average salary, average tenure.
Bar: attrition % by department, sorted descending.
Line: attrition % by month vs last year.
Matrix: job role by tenure band with attrition % as the value.

blocks.text: Explore age bands, gender, marital status, education field, and distance from home. Use a histogram for age and a scatter for distance versus attrition rate. Avoid decorative charts that make comparisons harder.
Compare environment, job, relationship, work-life, manager, and self ratings. Show distribution alongside average so a single mean does not hide a polarized team.

items: Sync the department and year slicers across all three pages.
Add a drill-through employee detail page.
Write finding-based titles on every visual.
Set alt text and tab order.
Add a hidden info page listing metric definitions and refresh time.

blocks.title: Final quality check
blocks.text: Test every slicer, title, tooltip, and cross-filter. Ask a colleague to explain one conclusion from each page without your help.

items: One question per page, shared filters across pages.
Show distribution next to averages for rating data.
A definitions page makes the report self-explanatory.

blocks.text: Publishing moves your model and report into the Service where other people can use it.

head: Role
Can do
rows: Publish and edit content, not share

blocks.text: For serious projects keep three workspaces — Development, Test, Production — and promote content between them. Parameters swap the data source per stage so a test refresh never hits production.

items: Never share from My Workspace; use a shared workspace.
Apps give a clean, read-only experience for business users.
Dev/Test/Prod workspaces prevent accidental edits to live reports.

blocks.text: An import model is only as current as its last refresh. Configure it deliberately.

items: Publish the report to a shared workspace.
Open the semantic model settings and enter data source credentials.
Install and register the **on-premises data gateway** for local or on-prem sources.
Set the schedule, time zone, and failure notification recipients.
Add a “Last refreshed” measure to the report so users can see data currency.

blocks.code:
Last Refreshed =
"Data as of " & FORMAT ( MAX ( 'Refresh Log'[RefreshTime] ), "dd MMM yyyy HH:mm" )

items: Pro allows 8 scheduled refreshes per day; PPU and capacity allow 48.
Credential errors are the most common failure — re-enter them after a password change.
Local file paths break in the Service unless a gateway can reach them; prefer OneDrive, SharePoint, or a database.
Use incremental refresh for large fact tables instead of reloading history daily.
Gateways are required for anything not already in the cloud.
Show a refresh timestamp in the report itself.
Incremental refresh is the answer to slow full loads.

blocks.text: Two final production concerns: who can see which rows, and how fast the report responds.

items: In Desktop, **Modeling → Manage roles**, create a role and add a DAX filter.
Test with **View as role**.
Publish, then assign users or security groups to the role in the Service.

blocks.title: Important
blocks.text: RLS does not apply to workspace Admins, Members, or Contributors. Test with a Viewer account, and remember RLS filters rows — it does not hide columns or pages.

head: Lever
Action
Impact
rows: Remove unused columns and high-cardinality keys
Move logic to Power Query or measures

blocks.text: Use **Performance Analyzer** in Desktop to record a page refresh and see DAX query, visual render, and other durations per visual. Anything over roughly 2 seconds of DAX time deserves attention. DAX Studio and Tabular Editor go deeper when you need them.

blocks.text: Power BI interviews cluster around six themes. Prepare a crisp answer and one example for each.

head: Question
Answer shape
rows: Star: dimensions one hop from facts, simpler DAX, faster. Snowflake normalizes dimensions further; flatten where possible.
Column evaluates per row at refresh and is stored; measure evaluates at query time in filter context.
Contiguous dates enable time intelligence; mark as date table and turn off auto date/time.
Bridge table with single-direction relationships, or a many-to-many relationship where justified.

head: Question
Answer shape
rows: Modifies filter context by adding, removing, or replacing filters before evaluating an expression.
ALL/REMOVEFILTERS clear all filters; ALLSELECTED respects outer slicer selections.
SUM aggregates a column; SUMX iterates a table evaluating an expression per row.
Readability plus a single evaluation, avoiding repeated computation.

items: **Query folding** — steps pushed to the source as SQL; keep folding-breaking steps last.
**Import vs DirectQuery** — speed and full DAX vs freshness and source load.
**Incremental refresh** — partitions by date so only recent data reloads.
**RLS** — static and dynamic roles with USERPRINCIPALNAME; does not apply to workspace editors.
**Slow report** — Performance Analyzer, reduce visuals, fix the model, remove bi-directional filters.

blocks.text: Prepare one story about a stakeholder disagreeing with a number, and how you traced the definition back to the source. Interviewers weigh that more heavily than any function you can recite.
